name: History of Industrial Production
description: Iran’s industrial history includes the development of mechanized consumer-goods factories, heavy industry, and manufacturing supported by oil revenues. State investment, private enterprise, imported technology, revolution, and war shaped successive phases of production.

seo.title: History of Industrial Production in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How Iran developed modern manufacturing through consumer-goods factories, heavy industry, state investment, revolution, and reconstruction.

content.heading: From craft production to mechanized factories
content.content:
Modern factories did not emerge into an industrial vacuum. Before mechanization, Iranian production depended heavily on crafts, while machinery-based establishments remained uncommon. Hassan Hakimian’s historical account identifies weak transport connections, limited technical skills, and competition from lightly taxed imports among the obstacles to factory development. Industrialization therefore required more than purchasing machinery: it also depended on connecting markets and creating institutions capable of supporting production. [s1]

Under Reza Shah, who ruled from 1925 to 1941, the government moved from encouraging private investment toward more direct industrial intervention. Factories producing textiles, sugar, matches, and glass addressed existing consumer demand; cement and chemicals expanded the range of domestic production. Import substitution meant making goods at home that had previously been purchased abroad. [s1]

The new plants were not uniformly secure businesses. The Watan textile factory in Isfahan, for example, relied on government assistance and purchasing support. Wartime occupation and difficulties importing machinery subsequently disrupted industrial development during the 1940s. Establishing a factory and sustaining competitive production were different achievements. [s1]

content.heading: A larger industrial system
content.content:
After the early postwar expansion and the foreign-exchange crisis around 1960, industrial policy became more explicitly interventionist. Protection of the domestic market, access to finance, and public investment helped support manufacturing expansion. Import substitution changed the composition of imports rather than simply eliminating dependence on them: machinery and intermediate inputs became increasingly important. [s2]

During the later Pahlavi period, government investment concentrated on activities such as basic metals, mechanical engineering, chemicals, and petrochemicals. These required resources beyond the capacity of many private investors. Public infrastructure and heavy industry also supplied services, materials, and technical experience that could benefit private manufacturers. [s2]

Oil revenues helped finance this investment system. Their importance complicates any division between an oil economy and a manufacturing economy: petroleum income could support industrial diversification while making investment dependent on external earnings. The historical question is consequently not just whether factories multiplied, but how their financing, inputs, and markets fitted together. [s2]

content.heading: Ownership, war, and reconstruction
content.content:
The 1979 revolution transformed industrial ownership. Nationalization and transfers to foundations accompanied disruption caused by managerial departures, indebted enterprises, labor conflict, and uncertainty over control. Foundations, commonly called bonyads, became significant holders of productive assets alongside the state. These changes combined political redistribution with attempts to keep enterprises operating. [s3]

During the Iran–Iraq War, production faced competing claims on resources, restricted access to foreign exchange, and difficulties obtaining imported inputs. Parvin Alizadeh’s historical assessment also emphasizes domestic policy choices, including administered prices and preferential exchange rates. Her explanation treats wartime industrial difficulties as the interaction of external pressures and internal institutions. [s3]

Postwar development planning sought reconstruction and greater production of intermediate and capital goods. Announced investment priorities, however, were not proof of completed industrial transformation. Alizadeh notes limitations in the disaggregated evidence available for assessing outcomes. This history is best read through separate questions about capacity, actual output, ownership, and dependence on imported technology; one measure cannot establish all four. [s3]

name: History of Banking
description: Iranian banking developed from merchant finance into a system of foreign concessionary banks, Iranian-owned institutions, and specialized financial intermediaries. Revolution and subsequent reforms changed ownership and the legal framework, while later research documented differences between formal financial principles and banking practice.

seo.title: History of Banking in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: From merchant bankers and foreign concessions to Iranian-owned banks, nationalization, and the changing relationship between banking law and practice.

content.heading: Finance before the modern bank
content.content:
Finance existed before purpose-built banking institutions. Merchant bankers accepted deposits, transferred funds, and handled bills of exchange, while money dealers known as sarrafs supplied credit. These activities connected banking functions with commercial relationships rather than a separate nationwide banking organization. [s1]

The British-owned New Oriental Bank opened Iranian operations in 1888. The Imperial Bank of Persia followed in 1889 under a concession that included exclusive banknote-issuing rights. A Russian loan bank subsequently added another institution tied to a foreign power. Modern banking therefore developed within the unequal diplomatic and commercial relationships of the late Qajar period. [s1]

Iranian ownership changed that landscape. Bank Sepah began in 1925 with army pension resources, and the government-owned Bank Melli followed in 1928. Melli became central to mobilizing domestic funds. Later private banks and specialized lenders broadened the institutional landscape and the channels through which savings could reach investment. Potkin Basseer’s historical assessment nevertheless distinguishes expansion of finance from its distribution: credit serving government priorities did not necessarily provide equivalent opportunities for private borrowers. [s1]

content.heading: Revolution changed ownership and contracts
content.content:
The revolution brought nationalization and consolidation of banking institutions. A contemporaneous IMF account describes this reorganization as preceding the implementation of the Law of Usury-Free Banking. The law was passed in 1983, with implementation beginning in March 1984. These were distinct changes: nationalization concerned ownership, while the later framework concerned how financial transactions were structured. [s2]

This distinction matters when reading institutional histories. A bank can retain familiar functions such as accepting deposits and financing businesses while the legal language and contractual basis of those activities change. Conversely, adopting a new framework does not by itself establish how risk and returns are distributed in practice. The IMF account is evidence of the historical reform sequence, rather than verification of compliance by every bank. [s2]

content.heading: Formal principles and documented practice
content.content:
A 2019 Peterson Institute policy brief illustrates why legal descriptions need to be checked against banking behavior. Its authors described a substantial gap between formally prescribed Islamic financial principles and transactions that, in their assessment, often resembled conventional fixed-return banking. This is a dated analytical finding, not a statement that every institution or contract operated identically. [s3]

The same study examined competition from unlicensed financial institutions. Some attracted deposits with higher promised returns while operating outside adequate supervision. Subsequent intervention, liquidity support, closures, and transfers of assets and liabilities demonstrated that financial activity extended beyond the institutions visible in a conventional bank directory. [s3]

For readers exploring this history, the useful distinction is between who owns an institution, which contracts it formally uses, and how effectively it is supervised. None answers the others automatically. Banking history consequently concerns both the expansion of financial services and the recurring problem of making promises to depositors credible. The evidence presented here reaches into the late 2010s; it does not establish the condition of the banking system at the 2026 cutoff. [s3]

name: Money & Coinage
description: Iranian coinage records changing systems of exchange, royal authority, mint organization, and monetary terminology. Its history extends from Achaemenid gold and silver issues through Sasanian and Islamic currencies to the centralization of modern minting.

seo.title: Money and Coinage in Iranian History | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian coins as money and historical evidence, from the Achaemenid daric to Sasanian silver, Islamic inscriptions, and modern minting.

content.heading: The daric and imperial exchange
content.content:
A coin is both a means of payment and a manufactured statement of authority. The Achaemenid daric, introduced under Darius I toward the end of the sixth century BCE, paired gold coinage with the silver denomination known as the siglos. Michael Alram’s account traces this monetary arrangement to the earlier Lydian system rather than treating it as an invention without predecessors. [s1]

The recognizable figure carrying a bow helped give Persian coins a distinctive identity among Greek users. Yet the history of the word daric is less certain than a straightforward association with Darius might suggest: ancient explanations and modern linguistic interpretations differ. The coin’s physical design, circulation, and name therefore provide different kinds of evidence and need not yield equally certain conclusions. [s1]

content.heading: Reading Sasanian silver
content.content:
The Sasanian monetary system was dominated by the silver drachm. These coins were struck by hand, with a royal portrait on the front and, on many issues, a fire altar on the reverse. Such imagery belongs to the historical evidence of kingship and religious authority. It should be interpreted in that context rather than treated as generic decoration. [s2]

Mint signatures and regnal dates make many issues especially useful to historians. They can help reconstruct where production occurred and under whose authority, although abbreviated mint names and disputed attributions require specialist interpretation. The surviving material represents only a small part of the original output. A collection’s composition consequently cannot be read directly as a census of ancient economic activity. [s2]

Princeton’s Schaaf collection provides an accessible research entry point. It includes gold issues, fractional denominations, and copper and lead material alongside the better-known silver coinage. That variety helps prevent the most familiar surviving denomination from standing for an entire monetary system. [s3]

content.heading: Political change did not instantly replace the currency
content.content:
After the Arab conquest, coinage retained Sasanian features while inscriptions and issuing authorities changed. The resulting Arab-Sasanian issues demonstrate continuity across a major political transition. Later reforms introduced predominantly inscription-based Islamic gold and silver coins. Changes were not simultaneous everywhere: some eastern areas continued older-looking types after other mints had adopted the new designs. [s4]

This regional unevenness matters. A ruler’s accession, a conquest, and the disappearance of an earlier coin type are separate events. Coin evidence can refine political chronology, but it should not be forced into a model of immediate, uniform replacement. [s4]

content.heading: Modern minting and changing names
content.content:
Qajar monetary history combined changing standards with recognizable denomination names. The qeran became a principal silver denomination, while the toman appeared in gold coinage and monetary reckoning. These historical terms cannot safely be assigned one timeless metal content or purchasing power. [s4]

During the late nineteenth century, machinery imported from Europe supported centralized minting in Tehran and the suppression of provincial mints. Older hammered coins nevertheless remained in circulation. Technical modernization and the replacement of money already held by users were distinct processes. [s4]

The lesson for reading prices in historical accounts is practical: first identify the date, denomination, and monetary context. A familiar name alone cannot establish an equivalent modern value. This page leaves current currency law and any redenomination implementation unresolved pending direct legal verification.
